content: 1. The term PLHIV refers to individuals who are either confirmed to be HIV-positive or whose HIV status is unknown but present with strong clinical evidence of HIV infection. These individuals may reside in areas with a high prevalence of HIV or belong to groups at increased risk for HIV. For all individuals with unknown HIV status, HIV testing should be conducted in accordance with national guidelines. 2. PLHIV who also have tuberculosis (TB) may exhibit symptoms of extrapulmonary TB, such as lymphadenopathy, meningitis, or other atypical presentations that require further evaluation. 3. The definition of seriously ill is based on the presence of any of the following danger signs: a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths per minute, a temperature exceeding 39°C, a heart rate over 120 beats per minute, or the inability to walk unaided. 4. Advanced HIV disease (AHD) in adults, adolescents, and children aged over 5 years is defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO stage 3 or 4 event at the time of care presentation. All children under the age of 5 are considered to have AHD. 5. The LF-LAM test and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRD) should be performed simultaneously. LF-LAM results, which are available in less than 15 minutes, should guide initial treatment decisions while awaiting the results of other diagnostic tests. 6. Patients should be started on a first-line TB treatment regimen as per national guidelines unless they are at a very high risk of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). In such cases, an MDR-TB regimen should be initiated. Treatment regimens should be adjusted based on the results of mWRD testing. 7. A negative LF-LAM result does not exclude TB in symptomatic individuals. The mWRD results should be reviewed when available, and further clinical evaluations for TB should be conducted as necessary. 8. If both LF-LAM and mWRD results are negative, TB cannot be ruled out in symptomatic individuals. Additional investigations, such as chest X-rays, further clinical assessments, or repeat mWRD testing or culture, should be performed. Consider initiating treatment for bacterial infections with broad-spectrum antibiotics (excluding fluoroquinolones) and for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Clinical response should be reassessed after 3–5 days of treatment. 9. For hospitalized PLHIV being evaluated for TB, urine samples should be collected for LF-LAM testing, and appropriate specimens should be collected for mWRD testing. If mWRD is available on-site, it should be performed in parallel with LF-LAM testing. 10. For pulmonary TB evaluation, preferred samples for mWRD include induced or expectorated sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, gastric lavage, or aspirates. Additional sample types suitable for Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra include nasopharyngeal aspirates and stool samples. 11. For extrapulmonary TB evaluation, the Xpert MTB test is recommended for cerebrospinal fluid (preferred for TB meningitis), lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, or urine as initial diagnostic tests. Blood samples may also be used for HIV-positive adults and children with signs of disseminated TB. 12. All patients with a positive LF-LAM result should be started on TB treatment immediately while awaiting mWRD results. Therapy should be modified as needed based on mWRD results, including resistance detection. 13. If clinical improvement is observed after 3–5 days of treatment, reassess for TB and other HIV-related diseases. However, clinical improvement does not necessarily rule out TB. 14. For hospitalized PLHIV without TB symptoms but with AHD, serious illness, or a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³, urine LF-LAM testing should be conducted. If LF-LAM is positive, initiate TB treatment and collect specimens for mWRD testing to assess rifampicin resistance. 15. For PLHIV in outpatient settings, evaluate for TB, determine HIV status, and assess for AHD and danger signs of serious illness. Measure CD4 cell counts in those who are not seriously ill to determine eligibility for LF-LAM testing. 16. WHO recommends against using LF-LAM for diagnosing active TB in HIV-positive individuals without TB symptoms and with a CD4 count above 100 cells/mm³ in outpatient settings, as well as in HIV-negative individuals due to suboptimal sensitivity and specificity. 17. All patients with pulmonary TB symptoms capable of producing sputum should have at least one specimen submitted for mWRD testing. This includes children and adolescents living with HIV who can provide a sputum sample. 18. For hospitalized PLHIV with no TB symptoms and a CD4 count of 200 cells/mm³ or higher (or unknown), LF-LAM testing is not recommended. Instead, clinical management should follow national guidelines.
